title: COMP26020 PLP Mock Exam Quiz
description: A code-heavy 80 mark mock quiz covering C, compilation, C++, Haskell, Rust, and concurrency. Use the sidebar to track which questions are complete.

options: The allocation is one byte too small because it does not reserve space for the terminating `\0`.
The return value of `malloc` is not checked before `strcpy` writes through it.
The function must call `free(buf)` before returning to avoid a leak.
`strcpy` is safe here because `strlen(src)` gives exactly the number of visible characters.
If `src` is `NULL`, the call to `strlen(src)` is invalid before allocation even happens.

On typical unsigned arithmetic, `-1` becomes a very large unsigned value, so `not less` is plausible.

An explicit cast or avoiding mixed signed/unsigned comparison can make the programmer's intention clearer.

questions.text: Part II — Compilation (1 mark). The regex `(ab|a)*b` is used as a token pattern. Which input is accepted by the whole regex?

Part II — Compilation (2 marks). In subset construction, suppose the current DFA state is the NFA-state set `{0,2}`. You are given:

- `move({0,2}, a) = {1,3}`
- `ε-closure({1,3}) = {1,3,4}`
- `move({0,2}, b) = {2}`
- `ε-closure({2}) = {2,5}`

What DFA transition should be recorded on input `a`?

Part II — Compilation (2 marks). Consider this grammar.
```text
S -> if E then S else S
S -> if E then S
S -> id
```
Why is this difficult for a predictive `LL(1)` parser without rewriting or extra disambiguation rules?
options: Both `S` alternatives beginning with `if E then S` have the same initial lookahead sequence, so one token of lookahead cannot choose safely.
The grammar is regular, so it should be handled by the scanner rather than the parser.
The grammar has no terminals, so FIRST sets cannot be computed.
The grammar is bottom-up only because every grammar containing `else` is LR(1) but never LL(1).

```text

2: b = load B

```
options: the address/value `A` loaded at line 1 is necessarily live after line 4

questions.text:
Part II — Compilation (2 marks). Which optimisations are valid for this IR if no variable except `z` and `w` is used later?
```text
x = 2 * 3
y = x
z = y + 4
w = 2 * 3
```
options: Copy propagation can replace the use of `y` with the value copied from `x`.
Dead-code elimination can remove assignments to `x` and `y` after their useful values have been propagated.
The optimiser may replace `z` by `w` because both originally mention `2 * 3`.
Optimisation is allowed to change the printed output if the target code is shorter.

questions.text: Part II — Compilation (8 marks). Match each compiler concept to the best description.

matches.prompt: Turns a stream of characters into tokens such as identifiers, numbers, and operators.
Checks whether the token sequence can be generated by the grammar and builds parse structure.
Uses context such as types, declarations, and scopes to reject programs that parse but do not make sense.
Target-neutral code form such as three-address code, used between frontend and backend.
Replaces expressions like `3 + 4` with `7` when safe.
Replaces later uses of a copied variable with the original value where safe.
Stores a value in memory because there are not enough physical registers.
Reorders instructions subject to dependencies to reduce latency or improve pipeline use.

options: The call `p->value()` uses virtual dispatch and should call `Derived::value`.
Deleting a `Derived` object through `Base *` is unsafe here because `Base` does not have a virtual destructor.
The derived object acquires a heap resource in its constructor and attempts to release it in its destructor, which is an RAII-style pattern.
This code is safe because every class destructor is automatically virtual in C++.
Object slicing occurs at `Base *p = new Derived();` because the object is copied into a smaller `Base` object.

questions.text: Part III — C++ (2 marks). Match each C++ feature to the best description.

matches.prompt: An alias that must be initialised and cannot normally be reseated to another object.
An object that stores an address and may be null or reassigned.
Special member function used to initialise an object when its lifetime begins.
Special member function used to clean up when an object's lifetime ends.
`A *p = new B; p->f();` chooses `B::f` through a base pointer.
`g(3)` selects between `g(int)` and `g(double)` before runtime.
In `class Hidden { int x; };`, member `x` cannot be accessed from outside unless access is changed.

questions.text: Part IV — Haskell (2 marks). Which statements about Haskell IO are correct?
options: You cannot generally turn an `IO String` directly into a pure `String`; you must sequence the action using `>>=` or `do` notation.
In Haskell, `return x` wraps `x` into an IO/action context; it does not exit the function like C/Java `return`.
`main` should normally be a pure `String` because the runtime prints its value automatically.
Inside `do`, `name <- getLine` binds the result produced by the IO action for use in later IO actions.
The bind operator has type `IO a -> (a -> b) -> IO b`, so the function after bind can return a pure value.

questions.text:
Part IV — Haskell typing (3 marks). Fill the gaps in the type signatures. Use exactly the shown type-variable names.
```haskell
applyTwice f x = f (f x)
safeHead [] = Nothing
safeHead (x:_) = Just x
same x y = x == y

applyTwice :: ({t1}) -> a -> a
safeHead :: {t2} -> Maybe a
same :: {t3} => a -> a -> Bool
```

Part IV — Haskell strictness (3 marks). Write `bottom` for an expression that crashes, is undefined, or does not terminate.
```haskell
xs = [1, undefined, 3]
ys = 1 : undefined

a = head xs
b = length xs
c = length ys
```
Then `a` evaluates to {a_val}, `b` evaluates to {b_val}, and `c` evaluates to {c_val}.

Part IV — Haskell recursive problem (12 marks). A stage decoration is either a light of one colour or a fork containing a left and right decoration. A decoration is symmetric when its left and right sides mirror each other exactly, including leaf colours.
```haskell
data Colour = Red | Blue deriving (Eq, Show)
data Deco = Light Colour | Fork Deco Deco deriving (Eq, Show)
```
Three possible strategies are shown, as in the exam. In this JSON-app version, fill Program C only.

PROGRAM A — direct recursive strategy
```haskell
mirrorEq (Light x) (Light y) = x == y
mirrorEq (Fork a b) (Fork c d) = mirrorEq a d && mirrorEq b c
mirrorEq _ _ = False

symmetric (Light _) = True
symmetric (Fork l r) = mirrorEq l r
```

PROGRAM B — coordinate strategy
```haskell
-- collect each leaf together with its path from the root,
-- then compare every path with its opposite path.
```

PROGRAM C — convert the tree to a string and compare with its mirror
```haskell
mirrorChar '(' = {gap1}
mirrorChar ')' = {gap2}
mirrorChar c   = c

deco_to_string :: Deco -> String
deco_to_string (Light Red)  = "r"
deco_to_string (Light Blue) = "b"
deco_to_string (Fork l r) = {gap3} ++ deco_to_string l ++ deco_to_string r ++ {gap4}

mirror_string :: String -> String
mirror_string [] = []
mirror_string (c:cs) = mirror_string cs ++ [{gap5} c]

symmetric :: Deco -> Bool
symmetric d = deco_to_string d == {gap6} (deco_to_string d)
```

options: `x` starts living at line 4 and is dropped at the end of the inner block after line 6, so using `r` at line 8 would dangle.
`x` starts living at line 5 because references create the object, and it lasts until line 8 because `r` needs it.
The code is valid because lifetime annotations can always extend `x` until the final `println!`.
The only issue is that `String::from` should be replaced by a string literal; the reference lifetime is otherwise valid.
Ownership of the heap-allocated string is moved from `s` to `t` at `let t = s;`.
The `clone` creates a separate owned string for `u` rather than moving out of `t`.

`String` behaves like `i32`, so assignment silently copies the whole value and both `s` and `t` remain owners of the same allocation.
After `let u = t.clone();`, `t` is always invalid because `clone` consumes its receiver.
Having `a` and `b` as simultaneous immutable borrows is allowed.
The mutable borrow `c` is allowed after the last use of `a` and `b` under non-lexical lifetimes.
If `println!("{} {}", a, b);` were moved after `let c = &mut s;`, the code would violate Rust's borrowing rules.
Rust allows any number of mutable borrows as long as they are not printed.
The variable `s` must be declared `mut` because `c.push_str` mutates the owned string through a mutable borrow.
